Question: A large sphere is on a horizontal field on a sunny day. At a certain time the shadow of the sphere reaches out a distance of \(10\) m from the point where the sphere touches the ground. At the same instant a meter stick (held vertically with one end on the ground) casts a shadow of length \(2\) m. What is the radius of the sphere in meters? (Assume the sun’s rays are parallel and the meter stick is a line segment.)
Solution:
Method 1: Use tangent lengths and similar triangles

We can work in the vertical plane through the sphere’s center along the shadow direction. Indeed, each horizontal slice of the sphere projects to a ground disk whose center is shifted along that direction; the point of each disk farthest from the ground contact lies in this plane.

Let \(O\) be the ground contact, \(C\) the sphere’s center, \(S\) the far shadow tip, and \(r>0\) the radius. Then \(CO=r\) and \(OS=10\). The boundary ray from \(S\) touches the circular cross-section at a point \(T\). A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at its point of contact, so triangles \(COS\) and \(CTS\) are right triangles. By the Pythagorean theorem,
\[
ST^2=CS^2-r^2=OS^2=100,
\]
so \(ST=10\).

The meter stick shows that a ray rises 1 unit for every 2 units of horizontal travel. Its corresponding right triangle has hypotenuse \(\sqrt5\). Thus the horizontal length along \(TS\) is \(20/\sqrt5\). Since \(CT\) is perpendicular to the ray, its horizontal-to-vertical ratio is \(1:2\), and its horizontal length is \(r/\sqrt5\).

The upper tangent point \(T\) lies above and toward the shadow side of \(C\). Therefore these two horizontal lengths add to \(OS\):
\[
10=\frac{r}{\sqrt5}+\frac{20}{\sqrt5}.
\]
It follows that
\[
r=10\sqrt5-20>0.
\]
The radius is \(\boxed{10\sqrt5-20}\) meters, choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).

Method 2: Reflect the ray and compare areas

Consider the vertical cross-section through the sphere’s center along the rays. It contains the farthest shadow tip because the sphere’s horizontal slices project to disks centered along the shadow direction.

Let \(O\) be the ground contact, \(S\) the shadow tip with \(OS=10\), and \(C\) the center of the circular cross-section, of radius \(r\). The upper boundary ray through \(S\) is tangent to this circle. The meter stick gives a horizontal-to-vertical ray ratio of \(2:1\), so extending this ray backward to the vertical line through \(O\) reaches a point \(V\) at height 5.

Reflect the boundary ray across that vertical line. Reflection preserves the circle, so the reflected line is also tangent to it. It meets the ground at a point \(S'\) located 10 meters on the other side of \(O\). The circle is therefore inside triangle \(VS'S\), tangent to all three sides.

This triangle has base 20, height 5, and equal sloping sides
\[
\sqrt{10^2+5^2}=5\sqrt5.
\]
Its area is \(20\cdot5/2=50\). Joining \(C\) to its three vertices divides it into three triangles. Each has altitude \(r\), since a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at contact. Adding their areas gives
\[
50=\frac r2\left(20+10\sqrt5\right).
\]
Hence
\[
r=\frac{10}{2+\sqrt5}
=\frac{10(\sqrt5-2)}{5-4}
=10\sqrt5-20.
\]
The radius is \(\boxed{10\sqrt5-20}\) meters, choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
